The '''''Barbel''-class submarines''', the last [[Diesel-electric transmission|diesel-electric]] propelled [[attack submarine]]s built by the [[United States Navy]], incorporated numerous, radical engineering improvements over previous classes. They were the first production warships built with the teardrop-shape hull first tested on the experimental {{USS|Albacore|AGSS-569|6}}, and the first to combine the control room, attack center, and conning tower in the same space in the hull. They were of double hull design with 1.5-inch thick HY80 steel.  This class of submarine became part of the United States Navy's fleet in 1959 and was taken out of service 1988–1990, leaving the Navy with an entirely nuclear-powered submarine fleet.

The ''Barbel'' class' design is considered to be very effective.<ref>Polmar, Norman and Moore, K. J. (2004). ''Cold War Submarines: The Design and Construction of U.S. and Soviet Submarines, 1945–2001''. Dulles: Potomac Books. {{ISBN|978-1-57488-594-1}}, p. 215</ref> The {{sclass|Zwaardvis|submarine|1}}s of the [[Royal Netherlands Navy|Netherlands]] and the {{sclass|Hai Lung|submarine|4}} of the [[Republic of China Navy|Republic of China]] (designed and built in the Netherlands) were closely derived from the ''Barbel'' class design. The [[Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force|Japanese]] {{sclass|Uzushio|submarine|4}} and its successors were also influenced by the ''Barbel'' class.

==Design==
Designed under project [[Ship Characteristics Board|SCB 150]],<ref name="FriedmanSubs1" /> the class overall was a somewhat smaller diesel-powered version of the {{sclass|Skipjack|submarine|0}} [[nuclear submarine]]s, the first of which entered service only three months after ''Barbel'', having been laid down only 11 days later. Several features of the experimental {{USS|Albacore|AGSS-569|2}} were used in the ''Barbel''-class design, most obviously the fully streamlined "teardrop" hull. ''Albacore''{{'}}s single-shaft configuration, necessary to minimize drag and thus maximize speed, was also adopted for the ''Barbel''s, ''Skipjack''s, and all subsequent US nuclear submarines. This was a matter of considerable debate and analysis within the Navy, as two shafts offered redundancy and improved maneuverability.<ref name="FriedmanSubs1" /> For the first time, the ''Barbel''s also did away with the conning tower, instead combining the functions of attack center and control room into the same space, another feature adopted for all subsequent US submarines. This was facilitated by the adoption of "push-button" ballast control, another feature of ''Albacore''.<ref name="FriedmanSubs1" /> Previous designs had routed the trim system piping through the control room, where the valves were manually operated. The "push-button" system used hydraulic operators on each valve, remotely electrically operated (actually via toggle switches) from the control room. This greatly conserved control room space and reduced the time required to conduct trim operations. The overall layout made coordination of the weapons and ship control systems easier during combat operations.

The [[torpedo tube]] arrangement of the ''Barbel''s was the same as the ''Skipjack''s{{'}}, with six bow tubes in a three-over-three configuration. These (and the ''Skipjack''-derived [[George Washington-class submarine|''George Washington''-class SSBNs]]) were the only US Navy classes to have this configuration, as subsequent SSN designs used four angled midships torpedo tubes to make room for a large bow sonar sphere, and most SSBNs had four bow tubes.{{Citation needed|date=May 2026}}

The ''Barbel''s were built with bow mounted [[diving plane]]s, but these were replaced by sail planes (aka fairwater planes) within a few years. This feature was standard on US Navy submarines until bow planes returned with the improved {{sclass|Los Angeles|submarine|4}}, the first of which was launched in 1987.{{Citation needed|date=May 2026}}

'''USS ''Nautilus'' (SSN-571)''' was the world's first [[nuclear-powered ship|nuclear-powered boat]], [[nuclear-powered submarine]], and the first submarine to complete a submerged transit of the [[North Pole]] on 3 August 1958.  Her initial commanding officer was [[Eugene Parks Wilkinson|Eugene "Dennis" Wilkinson]], a widely respected naval officer who set the stage for many of the protocols of today's Nuclear Navy in the US and who had a storied career during military service and afterwards.<ref>Winters, Ann (28 March 2017). "Underway on Nuclear Power" -- The Man Behind the Words: Eugene P. "Dennis" Wilkinson, Vice Admiral USN. The American Nuclear Society.</ref>

''Nautilus'' shares the name of the [[Nautilus (fictional submarine)|fictional submarine]] in [[Jules Verne]]'s classic 1870 science fiction novel ''[[Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas]]''<ref name="20,000 Leagues Under the Seas">{{cite wikisource |last=Verne |first=Jules |translator=Frederick Paul Walter |title=20,000 Leagues Under the Seas |wslink=20,000 Leagues Under the Seas (Walter) |orig-date=1870 |noicon=yes}}</ref> and the {{USS|Nautilus|SS-168}} that served with distinction in [[World War II]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Nautilus III (SS-168) |url=https://www.history.navy.mil/content/history/nhhc/research/histories/ship-histories/danfs/n/nautilus-ss-168-iii.html |access-date=2021-01-17 |website=NHHC |language=en-US }}</ref>

The ''Nautilus'' was authorized in 1951. Construction began in 1952, and it was launched in January 1954, sponsored by [[Mamie Eisenhower]], wife of President [[Dwight D. Eisenhower]]. It was commissioned the following September into the [[United States Navy]] and was delivered to the Navy in 1955.

Her [[nuclear propulsion]] allowed her to remain submerged far longer than [[Diesel–electric powertrain|diesel-electric]] submarines, and she broke many records in her first years of operation and traveled to locations previously beyond the limits of submarines. In operation, she revealed a number of limitations in her design and construction, and this information was used to improve subsequent submarines.

''Nautilus'' was decommissioned in 1980 and designated a [[National Historic Landmark]] in 1982. She has been preserved as a [[museum ship]] at the [[Submarine Force Library and Museum]] in [[Groton, Connecticut]], where she receives around 250,000 visitors per year.

==Planning and construction==
[[File:Hyman Rickover inspecting USS Nautilus.jpg|thumb|Admiral [[Hyman G. Rickover]] aboard the ''Nautilus'']]
[[File:nautiluscore.jpg|thumb|upright|left|Launching ''Nautilus'']]

The conceptual design of the first nuclear submarine began in March 1950 as project [[Ship Characteristics Board|SCB 64]].<ref>Friedman, Submarines, pp 182</ref><ref>Hewlett & Duncan, Nuclear Navy, pp. 162</ref> In July 1951, Congress authorized the construction of a nuclear-powered submarine for the [[United States Navy|U.S. Navy]], which was planned and personally supervised by Captain [[Hyman G. Rickover]], known as the "Father of the Nuclear Navy."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.history.navy.mil/bios/rickover.htm |publisher=[[Naval History & Heritage Command]] |title=Biography of Admiral Hyman G. Rickover|access-date=6 September 2012|archive-date=10 February 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120210172002/http://www.history.navy.mil/bios/rickover.htm}}</ref> On 12 December 1951, the Department of the Navy announced that the submarine would be called ''Nautilus'', the fourth U.S. Navy vessel to bear the name.  The boat carried the [[Hull classification symbol|hull number]] SSN-571.<ref name = DANFS>{{cite web |url=https://www.history.navy.mil/research/histories/ship-histories/danfs/n/nautilus-ssn-571-iv.html |title=Nautilus IV (SSN-571) |work=[[Dictionary of American Naval Fighting Ships]] |year=1970 |publisher=[[Naval History & Heritage Command]]}}</ref>

Designers drew inspiration from the advanced hydrodynamic hull design of the [[Type XXI submarine|German Type XXI U-boat]] developed during World War II. The Type XXI U-boat featured a streamlined shape, which enabled greater underwater speed and efficiency compared to earlier submarine designs that were primarily optimized for surface travel. Its revolutionary approach to underwater performance influenced post-war submarine development worldwide, including the U.S. Navy's decision to focus on fully submerged operations.

[[File:nautilus core.jpg|thumb|upright|left|''Nautilus''{{'}}s reactor core prototype at the S1W facility in Idaho]]

''Nautilus''{{'}}s keel was laid at [[General Dynamics]]' Electric Boat Division in [[Groton, Connecticut]] by [[Harry S. Truman]] on 14 June 1952.<ref>{{Cite AV media |year=1952 |title=Video: Atom Sub. President Officiates At Laying Of Keel, 1952/06/16 (1952) |url=https://archive.org/details/1952-06-16_Atom_Sub |publisher=Universal Newsreels}}</ref> She was christened on 21 January 1954 and launched into the [[Thames River (Connecticut)|Thames River]], sponsored by [[Mamie Eisenhower]]. ''Nautilus'' was [[ship commissioning|commissioned]] on 30 September 1954 under the command of Commander [[Eugene P. Wilkinson]].<ref name = DANFS/>

''Nautilus'' was powered by the Submarine Thermal Reactor (STR), later designated the [[S2W reactor]], a [[pressurized water reactor]] produced for the US Navy by [[Westinghouse Electric Corporation]]. [[Bettis Atomic Power Laboratory]] developed the basic reactor plant design used in ''Nautilus'' after being given the assignment on 31 December 1947 to design a nuclear power plant for a submarine.<ref>{{cite press release |url=http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/hn/news960121.shtml |title=Lab's early submarine reactor program paved the way for modern nuclear power plants |work=Argonne's Nuclear Science and Technology Legacy |date=21 January 1996 |publisher=Argonne National Laboratory |access-date=6 September 2012}}</ref> Nuclear power had a crucial advantage in submarine propulsion because it is a zero-emission process that consumes no air. This design is the basis for nearly all of the US nuclear-powered submarines and surface combat ships, and was adapted by other countries for naval nuclear propulsion. The first actual prototype for ''Nautilus'' was constructed and tested by the [[Argonne National Laboratory]] in 1953 at [[S1W reactor|S1W]] at the [[Naval Reactors Facility]], part of the [[Idaho National Laboratory|National Reactor Testing Station]] in Idaho.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/hn/news960121.shtml |title=Argonne National Laboratory News Release, 21 January 1996, retrieved 31 December 2014 |access-date=3 May 2012 |archive-date=27 April 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170427064440/http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/hn/news960121.shtml |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/reactors/lwr3.shtml |title=Reactors designed by Argonne National Laboratory, retrieved 31 December 2014 |access-date=1 January 2015 |archive-date=22 June 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120622185310/http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/reactors/lwr3.shtml |url-status=live }}</ref>

=="Underway on nuclear power"==
Nautilus remained dockside after her commissioning for further construction and testing.  At 11:00 a.m. January 17, 1955, the crew dropped the mooring lines and Wilkinson, on the bridge with Rickover, gave the command to back.  When the boat was scarcely clear of the pier, the engineering officer in the maneuvering room reported to Wilkinson on the bridge that there was a loud noise in the starboard reduction gear and that he had switched to electrical propulsion. Under normal circumstances, Wilkinson would have returned at once to the dock, but in full view of the press boats and other small craft attracted to the scene, Rickover was determined not to terminate the trial unless it was necessary.  While the boat proceeded down the river on the port propeller alone, Panoff and the engineering officer inspected the noisy gear.  It took but a few minutes to replace a loose locking pin on a retaining nut, and Wilkinson shifted back to steam propulsion.  As the Nautilus slipped down the Thames past the breakwater into [[Long Island Sound]], a [[Signalman|signalman]] on the submarine blinked to the escort tug [[USS Skylark (ASR-20)|Skylark]]: "Underway on nuclear power."<ref>{{cite web |last=Hewlett/Duncan |first=Richard/Francis |date=June 25, 1973 |title=Nuclear Navy 1946-1962. Richard G. Hewlett and Francis Duncan page 218 |url=https://www.energy.gov/lm/articles/hewlett-and-duncan-nuclear-navy-1946-1962 |access-date=July 22, 2025 |website=energy.gov}}</ref> On 10 May, she headed south for her [[shakedown cruise]]. She traveled {{cvt|1100|nmi|km smi|lk=on|sp=us}} from [[Naval Submarine Base New London|New London]] to [[San Juan, Puerto Rico]] and covered {{cvt|1200|nmi|km smi|sp=us}} in less than 90 hours,<!--(sources differ: 84 hours or 89.8 hours) (I am fact-checking this with USN historian at Groton's Submarine Force Library and Museum --[[User:Pedant]])--><!--Since this is a speed of advance of only 13.33 knots, it's entirely believable --[[User:RobDuch]]--> submerged the entire way. This was the longest submerged cruise by a submarine at the time and at the highest sustained speed ever recorded.{{Citation_needed|date=August 2019}}
[[File:SS-571-Nautilus-trials.gif|thumb|USS ''Nautilus'' during its initial sea trials, 20 January 1955]]

From 1955 to 1957, ''Nautilus'' continued to be used to investigate the effects of increased submerged speeds and endurance. These improvements rendered the progress made in [[anti-submarine warfare]] during [[World War II]] virtually obsolete. [[Radar]] and [[maritime patrol aircraft|anti-submarine aircraft]] had proved crucial in defeating submarines during the war, but they proved ineffective against a vessel able to move quickly out of an area, change depth quickly, and stay submerged for very long periods.<ref>Friedman, Submarines, pp 109</ref>

[[File:GWBridgeUSSNautilus.agr.jpg|thumb|''Nautilus'' passes under the [[George Washington Bridge]] during a visit to [[New York Harbor]] in 1956]]

''Nautilus'' returned to [[New London, Connecticut]] on 21 July and departed again on 19 August for her first voyage of {{cvt|1200|nmi|km smi|sp=us}} under the polar pack ice. She then headed for the Eastern Atlantic to participate in [[NATO]] [[Operation Strikeback|exercises]] and to conduct a tour of various British and French ports where she was inspected by defense personnel of those countries. She arrived back at New London on 28 October, underwent upkeep, and then conducted coastal operations until the spring.{{Citation_needed|date=August 2019}}

Eisenhower|President Eisenhower]] ordered the U.S. Navy to attempt a submarine transit of the North Pole as a technological showpiece following the Soviet Union's successful launch of [[Sputnik]].<ref name= IceDiariesFactSheet>{{cite web |url=http://ct.arrl.org/IceDiariesFactSheet.pdf |title=Fact Sheet – USS Nautilus and Voyage to North Pole, August 1958 |last=Anderson |first=William R |access-date=6 September 2012 |archive-date=30 March 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120330182429/http://ct.arrl.org/IceDiariesFactSheet.pdf }}</ref> On 25 April 1958, ''Nautilus'' was underway again for the West Coast under Commander [[William Anderson (naval officer)|William R. Anderson]]. She stopped at [[San Diego]], [[San Francisco]], and [[Seattle]], then began her history-making polar transit under "[[Operation Sunshine (USS Nautilus)|Operation Sunshine]]", leaving Seattle on 9 June. '''USS ''Nautilus'' (SSN-571)''' was the world's first [[nuclear-powered ship|nuclear-powered boat]], [[nuclear-powered submarine]], and the first submarine to complete a submerged transit of the [[North Pole]] on 3 August 1958.  Her initial commanding officer was [[Eugene Parks Wilkinson|Eugene "Dennis" Wilkinson]], a widely respected naval officer who set the stage for many of the protocols of today's Nuclear Navy in the US and who had a storied career during military service and afterwards.<ref>Winters, Ann (28 March 2017). "Underway on Nuclear Power" -- The Man Behind the Words: Eugene P. "Dennis" Wilkinson, Vice Admiral USN. The American Nuclear Society.</ref>

''Nautilus'' shares the name of the [[Nautilus (fictional submarine)|fictional submarine]] in [[Jules Verne]]'s classic 1870 science fiction novel ''[[Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas]]''<ref name="20,000 Leagues Under the Seas">{{cite wikisource |last=Verne |first=Jules |translator=Frederick Paul Walter |title=20,000 Leagues Under the Seas |wslink=20,000 Leagues Under the Seas (Walter) |orig-date=1870 |noicon=yes}}</ref> and the {{USS|Nautilus|SS-168}} that served with distinction in [[World War II]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Nautilus III (SS-168) |url=https://www.history.navy.mil/content/history/nhhc/research/histories/ship-histories/danfs/n/nautilus-ss-168-iii.html |access-date=2021-01-17 |website=NHHC |language=en-US }}</ref>

The ''Nautilus'' was authorized in 1951. Construction began in 1952, and it was launched in January 1954, sponsored by [[Mamie Eisenhower]], wife of President [[Dwight D. Eisenhower]]. It was commissioned the following September into the [[United States Navy]] and was delivered to the Navy in 1955.

Her [[nuclear propulsion]] allowed her to remain submerged far longer than [[Diesel–electric powertrain|diesel-electric]] submarines, and she broke many records in her first years of operation and traveled to locations previously beyond the limits of submarines. In operation, she revealed a number of limitations in her design and construction, and this information was used to improve subsequent submarines.

''Nautilus'' was decommissioned in 1980 and designated a [[National Historic Landmark]] in 1982. She has been preserved as a [[museum ship]] at the [[Submarine Force Library and Museum]] in [[Groton, Connecticut]], where she receives around 250,000 visitors per year.

==Planning and construction==
[[File:Hyman Rickover inspecting USS Nautilus.jpg|thumb|Admiral [[Hyman G. Rickover]] aboard the ''Nautilus'']]
[[File:nautiluscore.jpg|thumb|upright|left|Launching ''Nautilus'']]

The conceptual design of the first nuclear submarine began in March 1950 as project [[Ship Characteristics Board|SCB 64]].<ref>Friedman, Submarines, pp 182</ref><ref>Hewlett & Duncan, Nuclear Navy, pp. 162</ref> In July 1951, Congress authorized the construction of a nuclear-powered submarine for the [[United States Navy|U.S. Navy]], which was planned and personally supervised by Captain [[Hyman G. Rickover]], known as the "Father of the Nuclear Navy."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.history.navy.mil/bios/rickover.htm |publisher=[[Naval History & Heritage Command]] |title=Biography of Admiral Hyman G. Rickover|access-date=6 September 2012|archive-date=10 February 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120210172002/http://www.history.navy.mil/bios/rickover.htm}}</ref> On 12 December 1951, the Department of the Navy announced that the submarine would be called ''Nautilus'', the fourth U.S. Navy vessel to bear the name.  The boat carried the [[Hull classification symbol|hull number]] SSN-571.<ref name = DANFS>{{cite web |url=https://www.history.navy.mil/research/histories/ship-histories/danfs/n/nautilus-ssn-571-iv.html |title=Nautilus IV (SSN-571) |work=[[Dictionary of American Naval Fighting Ships]] |year=1970 |publisher=[[Naval History & Heritage Command]]}}</ref>

Designers drew inspiration from the advanced hydrodynamic hull design of the [[Type XXI submarine|German Type XXI U-boat]] developed during World War II. The Type XXI U-boat featured a streamlined shape, which enabled greater underwater speed and efficiency compared to earlier submarine designs that were primarily optimized for surface travel. Its revolutionary approach to underwater performance influenced post-war submarine development worldwide, including the U.S. Navy's decision to focus on fully submerged operations.

[[File:nautilus core.jpg|thumb|upright|left|''Nautilus''{{'}}s reactor core prototype at the S1W facility in Idaho]]

''Nautilus''{{'}}s keel was laid at [[General Dynamics]]' Electric Boat Division in [[Groton, Connecticut]] by [[Harry S. Truman]] on 14 June 1952.<ref>{{Cite AV media |year=1952 |title=Video: Atom Sub. President Officiates At Laying Of Keel, 1952/06/16 (1952) |url=https://archive.org/details/1952-06-16_Atom_Sub |publisher=Universal Newsreels}}</ref> She was christened on 21 January 1954 and launched into the [[Thames River (Connecticut)|Thames River]], sponsored by [[Mamie Eisenhower]]. ''Nautilus'' was [[ship commissioning|commissioned]] on 30 September 1954 under the command of Commander [[Eugene P. Wilkinson]].<ref name = DANFS/>

''Nautilus'' was powered by the Submarine Thermal Reactor (STR), later designated the [[S2W reactor]], a [[pressurized water reactor]] produced for the US Navy by [[Westinghouse Electric Corporation]]. [[Bettis Atomic Power Laboratory]] developed the basic reactor plant design used in ''Nautilus'' after being given the assignment on 31 December 1947 to design a nuclear power plant for a submarine.<ref>{{cite press release |url=http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/hn/news960121.shtml |title=Lab's early submarine reactor program paved the way for modern nuclear power plants |work=Argonne's Nuclear Science and Technology Legacy |date=21 January 1996 |publisher=Argonne National Laboratory |access-date=6 September 2012}}</ref> Nuclear power had a crucial advantage in submarine propulsion because it is a zero-emission process that consumes no air. This design is the basis for nearly all of the US nuclear-powered submarines and surface combat ships, and was adapted by other countries for naval nuclear propulsion. The first actual prototype for ''Nautilus'' was constructed and tested by the [[Argonne National Laboratory]] in 1953 at [[S1W reactor|S1W]] at the [[Naval Reactors Facility]], part of the [[Idaho National Laboratory|National Reactor Testing Station]] in Idaho.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/hn/news960121.shtml |title=Argonne National Laboratory News Release, 21 January 1996, retrieved 31 December 2014 |access-date=3 May 2012 |archive-date=27 April 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170427064440/http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/hn/news960121.shtml |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/reactors/lwr3.shtml |title=Reactors designed by Argonne National Laboratory, retrieved 31 December 2014 |access-date=1 January 2015 |archive-date=22 June 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120622185310/http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/reactors/lwr3.shtml |url-status=live }}</ref>

=="Underway on nuclear power"==
Nautilus remained dockside after her commissioning for further construction and testing.  At 11:00 a.m. January 17, 1955, the crew dropped the mooring lines and Wilkinson, on the bridge with Rickover, gave the command to back.  When the boat was scarcely clear of the pier, the engineering officer in the maneuvering room reported to Wilkinson on the bridge that there was a loud noise in the starboard reduction gear and that he had switched to electrical propulsion. Under normal circumstances, Wilkinson would have returned at once to the dock, but in full view of the press boats and other small craft attracted to the scene, Rickover was determined not to terminate the trial unless it was necessary.  While the boat proceeded down the river on the port propeller alone, Panoff and the engineering officer inspected the noisy gear.  It took but a few minutes to replace a loose locking pin on a retaining nut, and Wilkinson shifted back to steam propulsion.  As the Nautilus slipped down the Thames past the breakwater into [[Long Island Sound]], a [[Signalman|signalman]] on the submarine blinked to the escort tug [[USS Skylark (ASR-20)|Skylark]]: "Underway on nuclear power."<ref>{{cite web |last=Hewlett/Duncan |first=Richard/Francis |date=June 25, 1973 |title=Nuclear Navy 1946-1962. Richard G. Hewlett and Francis Duncan page 218 |url=https://www.energy.gov/lm/articles/hewlett-and-duncan-nuclear-navy-1946-1962 |access-date=July 22, 2025 |website=energy.gov}}</ref> On 10 May, she headed south for her [[shakedown cruise]]. She traveled {{cvt|1100|nmi|km smi|lk=on|sp=us}} from [[Naval Submarine Base New London|New London]] to [[San Juan, Puerto Rico]] and covered {{cvt|1200|nmi|km smi|sp=us}} in less than 90 hours,<!--(sources differ: 84 hours or 89.8 hours) (I am fact-checking this with USN historian at Groton's Submarine Force Library and Museum --[[User:Pedant]])--><!--Since this is a speed of advance of only 13.33 knots, it's entirely believable --[[User:RobDuch]]--> submerged the entire way. This was the longest submerged cruise by a submarine at the time and at the highest sustained speed ever recorded.{{Citation_needed|date=August 2019}}
[[File:SS-571-Nautilus-trials.gif|thumb|USS ''Nautilus'' during its initial sea trials, 20 January 1955]]

[[File:GWBridgeUSSNautilus.agr.jpg|thumb|''Nautilus'' passes under the [[George Washington Bridge]] during a visit to [[New York Harbor]] in 1956]]

'''USS ''Nautilus'' (SSN-571)''' was the world's first [[nuclear-powered ship|nuclear-powered boat]], [[nuclear-powered submarine]], and the first submarine to complete a submerged transit of the [[North Pole]] on 3 August 1958.  Her initial commanding officer was [[Eugene Parks Wilkinson|Eugene "Dennis" Wilkinson]], a widely respected naval officer who set the stage for many of the protocols of today's Nuclear Navy in the US and who had a storied career during military service and afterwards.<ref>Winters, Ann (28 March 2017). "Underway on Nuclear Power" -- The Man Behind the Words: Eugene P. "Dennis" Wilkinson, Vice Admiral USN. The American Nuclear Society.</ref>

''Nautilus'' shares the name of the [[Nautilus (fictional submarine)|fictional submarine]] in [[Jules Verne]]'s classic 1870 science fiction novel ''[[Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas]]''<ref name="20,000 Leagues Under the Seas">{{cite wikisource |last=Verne |first=Jules |translator=Frederick Paul Walter |title=20,000 Leagues Under the Seas |wslink=20,000 Leagues Under the Seas (Walter) |orig-date=1870 |noicon=yes}}</ref> and the {{USS|Nautilus|SS-168}} that served with distinction in [[World War II]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Nautilus III (SS-168) |url=https://www.history.navy.mil/content/history/nhhc/research/histories/ship-histories/danfs/n/nautilus-ss-168-iii.html |access-date=2021-01-17 |website=NHHC |language=en-US }}</ref>

The ''Nautilus'' was authorized in 1951. Construction began in 1952, and it was launched in January 1954, sponsored by [[Mamie Eisenhower]], wife of President [[Dwight D. Eisenhower]]. It was commissioned the following September into the [[United States Navy]] and was delivered to the Navy in 1955.

Her [[nuclear propulsion]] allowed her to remain submerged far longer than [[Diesel–electric powertrain|diesel-electric]] submarines, and she broke many records in her first years of operation and traveled to locations previously beyond the limits of submarines. In operation, she revealed a number of limitations in her design and construction, and this information was used to improve subsequent submarines.

''Nautilus'' was decommissioned in 1980 and designated a [[National Historic Landmark]] in 1982. She has been preserved as a [[museum ship]] at the [[Submarine Force Library and Museum]] in [[Groton, Connecticut]], where she receives around 250,000 visitors per year.

==Planning and construction==
[[File:Hyman Rickover inspecting USS Nautilus.jpg|thumb|Admiral [[Hyman G. Rickover]] aboard the ''Nautilus'']]
[[File:nautiluscore.jpg|thumb|upright|left|Launching ''Nautilus'']]

The conceptual design of the first nuclear submarine began in March 1950 as project [[Ship Characteristics Board|SCB 64]].<ref>Friedman, Submarines, pp 182</ref><ref>Hewlett & Duncan, Nuclear Navy, pp. 162</ref> In July 1951, Congress authorized the construction of a nuclear-powered submarine for the [[United States Navy|U.S. Navy]], which was planned and personally supervised by Captain [[Hyman G. Rickover]], known as the "Father of the Nuclear Navy."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.history.navy.mil/bios/rickover.htm |publisher=[[Naval History & Heritage Command]] |title=Biography of Admiral Hyman G. Rickover|access-date=6 September 2012|archive-date=10 February 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120210172002/http://www.history.navy.mil/bios/rickover.htm}}</ref> On 12 December 1951, the Department of the Navy announced that the submarine would be called ''Nautilus'', the fourth U.S. Navy vessel to bear the name.  The boat carried the [[Hull classification symbol|hull number]] SSN-571.<ref name = DANFS>{{cite web |url=https://www.history.navy.mil/research/histories/ship-histories/danfs/n/nautilus-ssn-571-iv.html |title=Nautilus IV (SSN-571) |work=[[Dictionary of American Naval Fighting Ships]] |year=1970 |publisher=[[Naval History & Heritage Command]]}}</ref>

Designers drew inspiration from the advanced hydrodynamic hull design of the [[Type XXI submarine|German Type XXI U-boat]] developed during World War II. The Type XXI U-boat featured a streamlined shape, which enabled greater underwater speed and efficiency compared to earlier submarine designs that were primarily optimized for surface travel. Its revolutionary approach to underwater performance influenced post-war submarine development worldwide, including the U.S. Navy's decision to focus on fully submerged operations.

[[File:nautilus core.jpg|thumb|upright|left|''Nautilus''{{'}}s reactor core prototype at the S1W facility in Idaho]]

''Nautilus''{{'}}s keel was laid at [[General Dynamics]]' Electric Boat Division in [[Groton, Connecticut]] by [[Harry S. Truman]] on 14 June 1952.<ref>{{Cite AV media |year=1952 |title=Video: Atom Sub. President Officiates At Laying Of Keel, 1952/06/16 (1952) |url=https://archive.org/details/1952-06-16_Atom_Sub |publisher=Universal Newsreels}}</ref> She was christened on 21 January 1954 and launched into the [[Thames River (Connecticut)|Thames River]], sponsored by [[Mamie Eisenhower]]. ''Nautilus'' was [[ship commissioning|commissioned]] on 30 September 1954 under the command of Commander [[Eugene P. Wilkinson]].<ref name = DANFS/>

''Nautilus'' was powered by the Submarine Thermal Reactor (STR), later designated the [[S2W reactor]], a [[pressurized water reactor]] produced for the US Navy by [[Westinghouse Electric Corporation]]. [[Bettis Atomic Power Laboratory]] developed the basic reactor plant design used in ''Nautilus'' after being given the assignment on 31 December 1947 to design a nuclear power plant for a submarine.<ref>{{cite press release |url=http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/hn/news960121.shtml |title=Lab's early submarine reactor program paved the way for modern nuclear power plants |work=Argonne's Nuclear Science and Technology Legacy |date=21 January 1996 |publisher=Argonne National Laboratory |access-date=6 September 2012}}</ref> Nuclear power had a crucial advantage in submarine propulsion because it is a zero-emission process that consumes no air. This design is the basis for nearly all of the US nuclear-powered submarines and surface combat ships, and was adapted by other countries for naval nuclear propulsion. The first actual prototype for ''Nautilus'' was constructed and tested by the [[Argonne National Laboratory]] in 1953 at [[S1W reactor|S1W]] at the [[Naval Reactors Facility]], part of the [[Idaho National Laboratory|National Reactor Testing Station]] in Idaho.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/hn/news960121.shtml |title=Argonne National Laboratory News Release, 21 January 1996, retrieved 31 December 2014 |access-date=3 May 2012 |archive-date=27 April 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170427064440/http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/hn/news960121.shtml |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/reactors/lwr3.shtml |title=Reactors designed by Argonne National Laboratory, retrieved 31 December 2014 |access-date=1 January 2015 |archive-date=22 June 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120622185310/http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/reactors/lwr3.shtml |url-status=live }}</ref>

=="Underway on nuclear power"==
Nautilus remained dockside after her commissioning for further construction and testing.  At 11:00 a.m. January 17, 1955, the crew dropped the mooring lines and Wilkinson, on the bridge with Rickover, gave the command to back.  When the boat was scarcely clear of the pier, the engineering officer in the maneuvering room reported to Wilkinson on the bridge that there was a loud noise in the starboard reduction gear and that he had switched to electrical propulsion. Under normal circumstances, Wilkinson would have returned at once to the dock, but in full view of the press boats and other small craft attracted to the scene, Rickover was determined not to terminate the trial unless it was necessary.  While the boat proceeded down the river on the port propeller alone, Panoff and the engineering officer inspected the noisy gear.  It took but a few minutes to replace a loose locking pin on a retaining nut, and Wilkinson shifted back to steam propulsion.  As the Nautilus slipped down the Thames past the breakwater into [[Long Island Sound]], a [[Signalman|signalman]] on the submarine blinked to the escort tug [[USS Skylark (ASR-20)|Skylark]]: "Underway on nuclear power."<ref>{{cite web |last=Hewlett/Duncan |first=Richard/Francis |date=June 25, 1973 |title=Nuclear Navy 1946-1962. Richard G. Hewlett and Francis Duncan page 218 |url=https://www.energy.gov/lm/articles/hewlett-and-duncan-nuclear-navy-1946-1962 |access-date=July 22, 2025 |website=energy.gov}}</ref> On 10 May, she headed south for her [[shakedown cruise]]. She traveled {{cvt|1100|nmi|km smi|lk=on|sp=us}} from [[Naval Submarine Base New London|New London]] to [[San Juan, Puerto Rico]] and covered {{cvt|1200|nmi|km smi|sp=us}} in less than 90 hours,<!--(sources differ: 84 hours or 89.8 hours) (I am fact-checking this with USN historian at Groton's Submarine Force Library and Museum --[[User:Pedant]])--><!--Since this is a speed of advance of only 13.33 knots, it's entirely believable --[[User:RobDuch]]--> submerged the entire way. This was the longest submerged cruise by a submarine at the time and at the highest sustained speed ever recorded.{{Citation_needed|date=August 2019}}
[[File:SS-571-Nautilus-trials.gif|thumb|USS ''Nautilus'' during its initial sea trials, 20 January 1955]]

From 1955 to 1957, ''Nautilus'' continued to be used to investigate the effects of increased submerged speeds and endurance. These improvements rendered the progress made in [[anti-submarine warfare]] during [[World War II]] virtually obsolete. [[Radar]] and [[maritime patrol aircraft|anti-submarine aircraft]] had proved crucial in defeating submarines during the war, but they proved ineffective against a vessel able to move quickly out of an area, change depth quickly, and stay submerged for very long periods.<ref>Friedman, Submarines, pp 109</ref>

On 4 February 1957, ''Nautilus'' logged her 60,000th nautical mile ({{cvt|60000|nmi|disp=output only}}), matching the endurance of the fictional [[Nautilus (Verne)|''Nautilus'']] described in [[Jules Verne]]'s novel ''Twenty Thousand Leagues Under The Sea''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.history.navy.mil/research/histories/ship-histories/danfs/n/nautilus-ssn-571-iv.html |title=Nautilus IV (SSN-571) |publisher=[[Naval History & Heritage Command]] |work=[[Dictionary of American Naval Fighting Ships]] |quote=On 4 February 1957, ''Nautilus'' logged her 60,000th nautical mile to bring to reality the achievements of her fictitious namesake in Jules Verne's ''20,000 Leagues Under the Sea.'' |access-date=6 September 2012}}</ref> In May, she departed for the Pacific Coast to participate in coastal exercises and the fleet exercise operation "Home Run," which acquainted units of the [[United States Pacific Fleet|Pacific Fleet]] with the capabilities of nuclear submarines.{{Citation_needed|date=August 2019}}

[[File:GWBridgeUSSNautilus.agr.jpg|thumb|''Nautilus'' passes under the [[George Washington Bridge]] during a visit to [[New York Harbor]] in 1956]]

''Nautilus'' returned to [[New London, Connecticut]] on 21 July and departed again on 19 August for her first voyage of {{cvt|1200|nmi|km smi|sp=us}} under the polar pack ice. She then headed for the Eastern Atlantic to participate in [[NATO]] [[Operation Strikeback|exercises]] and to conduct a tour of various British and French ports where she was inspected by defense personnel of those countries. She arrived back at New London on 28 October, underwent upkeep, and then conducted coastal operations until the spring.{{Citation_needed|date=August 2019}}

===Operation Sunshine – under the North Pole===
{{see also|Operation Sunshine (USS Nautilus)|label 1=Operation Sunshine}}
[[Dwight D. Eisenhower|President Eisenhower]] ordered the U.S. Navy to attempt a submarine transit of the North Pole as a technological showpiece following the Soviet Union's successful launch of [[Sputnik]].<ref name= IceDiariesFactSheet>{{cite web |url=http://ct.arrl.org/IceDiariesFactSheet.pdf |title=Fact Sheet – USS Nautilus and Voyage to North Pole, August 1958 |last=Anderson |first=William R |access-date=6 September 2012 |archive-date=30 March 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120330182429/http://ct.arrl.org/IceDiariesFactSheet.pdf }}</ref> On 25 April 1958, ''Nautilus'' was underway again for the West Coast under Commander [[William Anderson (naval officer)|William R. Anderson]]. She stopped at [[San Diego]], [[San Francisco]], and [[Seattle]], then began her history-making polar transit under "[[Operation Sunshine (USS Nautilus)|Operation Sunshine]]", leaving Seattle on 9 June. On 19 June, she entered the [[Chukchi Sea]] but was turned back by deep [[drift ice]] in those shallow waters. On 28 June, she arrived at [[Pearl Harbor]] to await better ice conditions.{{Citation_needed|date=August 2019}}

By 23 July, she set a course northward.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.submarinemuseum.org/nautilus/index.shtml |title=Submarine Force Museum, History of USS NAUTILUS (SSN 571) |access-date=10 June 2016 |archive-date=19 June 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160619060331/http://www.submarinemuseum.org/nautilus/index.shtml }}</ref> She submerged in the Barrow Sea Valley on 1 August, and she became the first watercraft to reach the geographic [[North Pole]] on 3 August at 2315 [[Eastern Time Zone|EDT]].<ref name="nautilus.org" /> The ability to navigate at extreme latitudes without surfacing was enabled by the technology of the North American Aviation N6A-1 [[Inertial Navigation System]], a naval modification of the N6A used in the [[SM-64 Navaho|Navaho]] cruise missile; it had been installed on ''Nautilus'' and {{USS|Skate|SSN-578|2}} after initial sea trials on {{USS|Compass Island|AG-153|6}} in 1957.<ref name="Autonetics INS">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1T0NbffwteoC&pg=PA71 |title=Steel Boats, Iron Men: History of the US Submarine Force |publisher=Turner |page=71 |isbn=978-1-56311-081-8 |year=1994 |access-date=6 Sept

This design is the basis for nearly all of the US nuclear-powered submarines and surface combat ships, and was adapted by other countries for naval nuclear propulsion. The first actual prototype for ''Nautilus'' was constructed and tested by the [[Argonne National Laboratory]] in 1953 at [[S1W reactor|S1W]] at the [[Naval Reactors Facility]], part of the [[Idaho National Laboratory|National Reactor Testing Station]] in Idaho.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/hn/news960121.shtml |title=Argonne National Laboratory News Release, 21 January 1996, retrieved 31 December 2014 |access-date=3 May 2012 |archive-date=27 April 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170427064440/http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/hn/news960121.shtml |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/reactors/lwr3.shtml |title=Reactors designed by Argonne National Laboratory, retrieved 31 December 2014 |access-date=1 January 2015 |archive-date=22 June 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120622185310/http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/reactors/lwr3.shtml |url-status=live }}</ref>

=="Underway on nuclear power"==
Nautilus remained dockside after her commissioning for further construction and testing.  At 11:00 a.m. January 17, 1955, the crew dropped the mooring lines and Wilkinson, on the bridge with Rickover, gave the command to back.  When the boat was scarcely clear of the pier, the engineering officer in the maneuvering room reported to Wilkinson on the bridge that there was a loud noise in the starboard reduction gear and that he had switched to electrical propulsion. Under normal circumstances, Wilkinson would have returned at once to the dock, but in full view of the press boats and other small craft attracted to the scene, Rickover was determined not to terminate the trial unless it was necessary.  While the boat proceeded down the river on the port propeller alone, Panoff and the engineering officer inspected the noisy gear.  It took but a few minutes to replace a loose locking pin on a retaining nut, and Wilkinson shifted back to steam propulsion.  As the Nautilus slipped down the Thames past the breakwater into [[Long Island Sound]], a [[Signalman|signalman]] on the submarine blinked to the escort tug [[USS Skylark (ASR-20)|Skylark]]: "Underway on nuclear power."<ref>{{cite web |last=Hewlett/Duncan |first=Richard/Francis |date=June 25, 1973 |title=Nuclear Navy 1946-1962. Richard G. Hewlett and Francis Duncan page 218 |url=https://www.energy.gov/lm/articles/hewlett-and-duncan-nuclear-navy-1946-1962 |access-date=July 22, 2025 |website=energy.gov}}</ref> On 10 May, she headed south for her [[shakedown cruise]]. She traveled {{cvt|1100|nmi|km smi|lk=on|sp=us}} from [[Naval Submarine Base New London|New London]] to [[San Juan, Puerto Rico]] and covered {{cvt|1200|nmi|km smi|sp=us}} in less than 90 hours,<!--(sources differ: 84 hours or 89.8 hours) (I am fact-checking this with USN historian at Groton's Submarine Force Library and Museum --[[User:Pedant]])--><!--Since this is a speed of advance of only 13.33 knots, it's entirely believable --[[User:RobDuch]]--> submerged the entire way. This was the longest submerged cruise by a submarine at the time and at the highest sustained speed ever recorded.{{Citation_needed|date=August 2019}}
[[File:SS-571-Nautilus-trials.gif|thumb|USS ''Nautilus'' during its initial sea trials, 20 January 1955]]

From 1955 to 1957, ''Nautilus'' continued to be used to investigate the effects of increased submerged speeds and endurance. These improvements rendered the progress made in [[anti-submarine warfare]] during [[World War II]] virtually obsolete. [[Radar]] and [[maritime patrol aircraft|anti-submarine aircraft]] had proved crucial in defeating submarines during the war, but they proved ineffective against a vessel able to move quickly out of an area, change depth quickly, and stay submerged for very long periods.<ref>Friedman, Submarines, pp 109</ref>

[[File:GWBridgeUSSNautilus.agr.jpg|thumb|''Nautilus'' passes under the [[George Washington Bridge]] during a visit to [[New York Harbor]] in 1956]]

''Nautilus'' returned to [[New London, Connecticut]] on 21 July and departed again on 19 August for her first voyage of {{cvt|1200|nmi|km smi|sp=us}} under the polar pack ice. She then headed for the Eastern Atlantic to participate in [[NATO]] [[Operation Strikeback|exercises]] and to conduct a tour of various British and French ports where she was inspected by defense personnel of those countries. She arrived back at New London on 28 October, underwent upkeep, and then conducted coastal operations until the spring.{{Citation_needed|date=August 2019}}

{{see also|Operation Sunshine (USS Nautilus)|label 1=Operation Sunshine}}
[[Dwight D. Eisenhower|President Eisenhower]] ordered the U.S. Navy to attempt a submarine transit of the North Pole as a technological showpiece following the Soviet Union's successful launch of [[Sputnik]].<ref name= IceDiariesFactSheet>{{cite web |url=http://ct.arrl.org/IceDiariesFactSheet.pdf |title=Fact Sheet – USS Nautilus and Voyage to North Pole, August 1958 |last=Anderson |first=William R |access-date=6 September 2012 |archive-date=30 March 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120330182429/http://ct.arrl.org/IceDiariesFactSheet.pdf }}</ref> On 25 April 1958, ''Nautilus'' was underway again for the West Coast under Commander [[William Anderson (naval officer)|William R. Anderson]]. She stopped at [[San Diego]], [[San Francisco]], and [[Seattle]], then began her history-making polar transit under "[[Operation Sunshine (USS Nautilus)|Operation Sunshine]]", leaving Seattle on 9 June. On 19 June, she entered the [[Chukchi Sea]] but was turned back by deep [[drift ice]] in those shallow waters. '''USS ''Nautilus'' (SSN-571)''' was the world's first [[nuclear-powered ship|nuclear-powered boat]], [[nuclear-powered submarine]], and the first submarine to complete a submerged transit of the [[North Pole]] on 3 August 1958.  Her initial commanding officer was [[Eugene Parks Wilkinson|Eugene "Dennis" Wilkinson]], a widely respected naval officer who set the stage for many of the protocols of today's Nuclear Navy in the US and who had a storied career during military service and afterwards.<ref>Winters, Ann (28 March 2017). "Underway on Nuclear Power" -- The Man Behind the Words: Eugene P. "Dennis" Wilkinson, Vice Admiral USN. The American Nuclear Society.</ref>

''Nautilus'' shares the name of the [[Nautilus (fictional submarine)|fictional submarine]] in [[Jules Verne]]'s classic 1870 science fiction novel ''[[Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas]]''<ref name="20,000 Leagues Under the Seas">{{cite wikisource |last=Verne |first=Jules |translator=Frederick Paul Walter |title=20,000 Leagues Under the Seas |wslink=20,000 Leagues Under the Seas (Walter) |orig-date=1870 |noicon=yes}}</ref> and the {{USS|Nautilus|SS-168}} that served with distinction in [[World War II]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Nautilus III (SS-168) |url=https://www.history.navy.mil/content/history/nhhc/research/histories/ship-histories/danfs/n/nautilus-ss-168-iii.html |access-date=2021-01-17 |website=NHHC |language=en-US }}</ref>

The ''Nautilus'' was authorized in 1951. Construction began in 1952, and it was launched in January 1954, sponsored by [[Mamie Eisenhower]], wife of President [[Dwight D. Eisenhower]]. It was commissioned the following September into the [[United States Navy]] and was delivered to the Navy in 1955.

Her [[nuclear propulsion]] allowed her to remain submerged far longer than [[Diesel–electric powertrain|diesel-electric]] submarines, and she broke many records in her first years of operation and traveled to locations previously beyond the limits of submarines. In operation, she revealed a number of limitations in her design and construction, and this information was used to improve subsequent submarines.

''Nautilus'' was decommissioned in 1980 and designated a [[National Historic Landmark]] in 1982. She has been preserved as a [[museum ship]] at the [[Submarine Force Library and Museum]] in [[Groton, Connecticut]], where she receives around 250,000 visitors per year.

Rickover]], known as the "Father of the Nuclear Navy."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.history.navy.mil/bios/rickover.htm |publisher=[[Naval History & Heritage Command]] |title=Biography of Admiral Hyman G. Rickover|access-date=6 September 2012|archive-date=10 February 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120210172002/http://www.history.navy.mil/bios/rickover.htm}}</ref> On 12 December 1951, the Department of the Navy announced that the submarine would be called ''Nautilus'', the fourth U.S. Navy vessel to bear the name.  The boat carried the [[Hull classification symbol|hull number]] SSN-571.<ref name = DANFS>{{cite web |url=https://www.history.navy.mil/research/histories/ship-histories/danfs/n/nautilus-ssn-571-iv.html |title=Nautilus IV (SSN-571) |work=[[Dictionary of American Naval Fighting Ships]] |year=1970 |publisher=[[Naval History & Heritage Command]]}}</ref>

Its revolutionary approach to underwater performance influenced post-war submarine development worldwide, including the U.S. Navy's decision to focus on fully submerged operations.

'''USS ''Nautilus'' (SSN-571)''' was the world's first [[nuclear-powered ship|nuclear-powered boat]], [[nuclear-powered submarine]], and the first submarine to complete a submerged transit of the [[North Pole]] on 3 August 1958.  Her initial commanding officer was [[Eugene Parks Wilkinson|Eugene "Dennis" Wilkinson]], a widely respected naval officer who set the stage for many of the protocols of today's Nuclear Navy in the US and who had a storied career during military service and afterwards.<ref>Winters, Ann (28 March 2017). "Underway on Nuclear Power" -- The Man Behind the Words: Eugene P. "Dennis" Wilkinson, Vice Admiral USN. The American Nuclear Society.</ref>

''Nautilus'' shares the name of the [[Nautilus (fictional submarine)|fictional submarine]] in [[Jules Verne]]'s classic 1870 science fiction novel ''[[Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas]]''<ref name="20,000 Leagues Under the Seas">{{cite wikisource |last=Verne |first=Jules |translator=Frederick Paul Walter |title=20,000 Leagues Under the Seas |wslink=20,000 Leagues Under the Seas (Walter) |orig-date=1870 |noicon=yes}}</ref> and the {{USS|Nautilus|SS-168}} that served with distinction in [[World War II]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Nautilus III (SS-168) |url=https://www.history.navy.mil/content/history/nhhc/research/histories/ship-histories/danfs/n/nautilus-ss-168-iii.html |access-date=2021-01-17 |website=NHHC |language=en-US }}</ref>

The ''Nautilus'' was authorized in 1951. Construction began in 1952, and it was launched in January 1954, sponsored by [[Mamie Eisenhower]], wife of President [[Dwight D. Eisenhower]]. It was commissioned the following September into the [[United States Navy]] and was delivered to the Navy in 1955.

Her [[nuclear propulsion]] allowed her to remain submerged far longer than [[Diesel–electric powertrain|diesel-electric]] submarines, and she broke many records in her first years of operation and traveled to locations previously beyond the limits of submarines. In operation, she revealed a number of limitations in her design and construction, and this information was used to improve subsequent submarines.

''Nautilus'' was decommissioned in 1980 and designated a [[National Historic Landmark]] in 1982. She has been preserved as a [[museum ship]] at the [[Submarine Force Library and Museum]] in [[Groton, Connecticut]], where she receives around 250,000 visitors per year.

==Planning and construction==
[[File:Hyman Rickover inspecting USS Nautilus.jpg|thumb|Admiral [[Hyman G. Rickover]] aboard the ''Nautilus'']]
[[File:nautiluscore.jpg|thumb|upright|left|Launching ''Nautilus'']]

The conceptual design of the first nuclear submarine began in March 1950 as project [[Ship Characteristics Board|SCB 64]].<ref>Friedman, Submarines, pp 182</ref><ref>Hewlett & Duncan, Nuclear Navy, pp. 162</ref> In July 1951, Congress authorized the construction of a nuclear-powered submarine for the [[United States Navy|U.S. Navy]], which was planned and personally supervised by Captain [[Hyman G. Rickover]], known as the "Father of the Nuclear Navy."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.history.navy.mil/bios/rickover.htm |publisher=[[Naval History & Heritage Command]] |title=Biography of Admiral Hyman G. Rickover|access-date=6 September 2012|archive-date=10 February 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120210172002/http://www.history.navy.mil/bios/rickover.htm}}</ref> On 12 December 1951, the Department of the Navy announced that the submarine would be called ''Nautilus'', the fourth U.S. Navy vessel to bear the name.  The boat carried the [[Hull classification symbol|hull number]] SSN-571.<ref name = DANFS>{{cite web |url=https://www.history.navy.mil/research/histories/ship-histories/danfs/n/nautilus-ssn-571-iv.html |title=Nautilus IV (SSN-571) |work=[[Dictionary of American Naval Fighting Ships]] |year=1970 |publisher=[[Naval History & Heritage Command]]}}</ref>

Designers drew inspiration from the advanced hydrodynamic hull design of the [[Type XXI submarine|German Type XXI U-boat]] developed during World War II. The Type XXI U-boat featured a streamlined shape, which enabled greater underwater speed and efficiency compared to earlier submarine designs that were primarily optimized for surface travel. Its revolutionary approach to underwater performance influenced post-war submarine development worldwide, including the U.S. Navy's decision to focus on fully submerged operations.

[[File:nautilus core.jpg|thumb|upright|left|''Nautilus''{{'}}s reactor core prototype at the S1W facility in Idaho]]

''Nautilus''{{'}}s keel was laid at [[General Dynamics]]' Electric Boat Division in [[Groton, Connecticut]] by [[Harry S. Truman]] on 14 June 1952.<ref>{{Cite AV media |year=1952 |title=Video: Atom Sub. President Officiates At Laying Of Keel, 1952/06/16 (1952) |url=https://archive.org/details/1952-06-16_Atom_Sub |publisher=Universal Newsreels}}</ref> She was christened on 21 January 1954 and launched into the [[Thames River (Connecticut)|Thames River]], sponsored by [[Mamie Eisenhower]]. ''Nautilus'' was [[ship commissioning|commissioned]] on 30 September 1954 under the command of Commander [[Eugene P. Wilkinson]].<ref name = DANFS/>

''Nautilus'' was powered by the Submarine Thermal Reactor (STR), later designated the [[S2W reactor]], a [[pressurized water reactor]] produced for the US Navy by [[Westinghouse Electric Corporation]]. [[Bettis Atomic Power Laboratory]] developed the basic reactor plant design used in ''Nautilus'' after being given the assignment on 31 December 1947 to design a nuclear power plant for a submarine.<ref>{{cite press release |url=http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/hn/news960121.shtml |title=Lab's early submarine reactor program paved the way for modern nuclear power plants |work=Argonne's Nuclear Science and Technology Legacy |date=21 January 1996 |publisher=Argonne National Laboratory |access-date=6 September 2012}}</ref> Nuclear power had a crucial advantage in submarine propulsion because it is a zero-emission process that consumes no air. This design is the basis for nearly all of the US nuclear-powered submarines and surface combat ships, and was adapted by other countries for naval nuclear propulsion. The first actual prototype for ''Nautilus'' was constructed and tested by the [[Argonne National Laboratory]] in 1953 at [[S1W reactor|S1W]] at the [[Naval Reactors Facility]], part of the [[Idaho National Laboratory|National Reactor Testing Station]] in Idaho.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/hn/news960121.shtml |title=Argonne National Laboratory News Release, 21 January 1996, retrieved 31 December 2014 |access-date=3 May 2012 |archive-date=27 April 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170427064440/http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/hn/news960121.shtml |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/reactors/lwr3.shtml |title=Reactors designed by Argonne National Laboratory, retrieved 31 December 2014 |access-date=1 January 2015 |archive-date=22 June 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120622185310/http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/reactors/lwr3.shtml |url-status=live }}</ref>

=="Underway on nuclear power"==
Nautilus remained dockside after her commissioning for further construction and testing.  At 11:00 a.m. January 17, 1955, the crew dropped the mooring lines and Wilkinson, on the bridge with Rickover, gave the command to back.  When the boat was scarcely clear of the pier, the engineering officer in the maneuvering room reported to Wilkinson on the bridge that there was a loud noise in the starboard reduction gear and that he had switched to electrical propulsion. Under normal circumstances, Wilkinson would have returned at once to the dock, but in full view of the press boats and other small craft attracted to the scene, Rickover was determined not to terminate the trial unless it was necessary.  While the boat proceeded down the river on the port propeller alone, Panoff and the engineering officer inspected the noisy gear.  It took but a few minutes to replace a loose locking pin on a retaining nut, and Wilkinson shifted back to steam propulsion.  As the Nautilus slipped down the Thames past the breakwater into [[Long Island Sound]], a [[Signalman|signalman]] on the submarine blinked to the escort tug [[USS Skylark (ASR-20)|Skylark]]: "Underway on nuclear power."<ref>{{cite web |last=Hewlett/Duncan |first=Richard/Francis |date=June 25, 1973 |title=Nuclear Navy 1946-1962. Richard G. Hewlett and Francis Duncan page 218 |url=https://www.energy.gov/lm/articles/hewlett-and-duncan-nuclear-navy-1946-1962 |access-date=July 22, 2025 |website=energy.gov}}</ref> On 10 May, she headed south for her [[shakedown cruise]]. She traveled {{cvt|1100|nmi|km smi|lk=on|sp=us}} from [[Naval Submarine Base New London|New London]] to [[San Juan, Puerto Rico]] and covered {{cvt|1200|nmi|km smi|sp=us}} in less than 90 hours,<!--(sources differ: 84 hours or 89.8 hours) (I am fact-checking this with USN historian at Groton's Submarine Force Library and Museum --[[User:Pedant]])--><!--Since this is a speed of advance of only 13.33 knots, it's entirely believable --[[User:RobDuch]]--> submerged the entire way. This was the longest submerged cruise by a submarine at the time and at the highest sustained speed ever recorded.{{Citation_needed|date=August 2019}}
[[File:SS-571-Nautilus-trials.gif|thumb|USS ''Nautilus'' during its initial sea trials, 20 January 1955]]

From 1955 to 1957, ''Nautilus'' continued to be used to investigate the effects of increased submerged speeds and endurance. These improvements rendered the progress made in [[anti-submarine warfare]] during [[World War II]] virtually obsolete. [[Radar]] and [[maritime patrol aircraft|anti-submarine aircraft]] had proved crucial in defeating submarines during the war, but they proved ineffective against a vessel able to move quickly out of an area, change depth quickly, and stay submerged for very long periods.<ref>Friedman, Submarines, pp 109</ref>

On 4 February 1957, ''Nautilus'' logged her 60,000th nautical mile ({{cvt|60000|nmi|disp=output only}}), matching the endurance of the fictional [[Nautilus (Verne)|''Nautilus'']] described in [[Jules Verne]]'s novel ''Twenty Thousand Leagues Under The Sea''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.history.navy.mil/research/histories/ship-histories/danfs/n/nautilus-ssn-571-iv.html |title=Nautilus IV (SSN-571) |publisher=[[Naval History & Heritage Command]] |work=[[Dictionary of American Naval Fighting Ships]] |quote=On 4 February 1957, ''Nautilus'' logged her 60,000th nautical mile to bring to reality the achievements of her fictitious namesake in Jules Verne's ''20,000 Leagues Under the Sea.'' |access-date=6 September 2012}}</ref> In May, she departed for the Pacific Coast to participate in coastal exercises and the fleet exercise operation "Home Run," which acquainted units of the [[United States Pacific Fleet|Pacific Fleet]] with the capabilities of nuclear submarines.{{Citation_needed|date=August 2019}}

[[File:GWBridgeUSSNautilus.agr.jpg|thumb|''Nautilus'' passes under the [[George Washington Bridge]] during a visit to [[New York Harbor]] in 1956]]

''Nautilus'' returned to [[New London, Connecticut]] on 21 July and departed again on 19 August for her first voyage of {{cvt|1200|nmi|km smi|sp=us}} under the polar pack ice. She then headed for the Eastern Atlantic to participate in [[NATO]] [[Operation Strikeback|exercises]] and to conduct a tour of various British and French ports where she was inspected by defense personnel of those countries. She arrived back at New London on 28 October, underwent upkeep, and then conducted coastal operations until the spring.{{Citation_needed|date=August 2019}}

===Operation Sunshine – under the North Pole===
{{see also|Operation Sunshine (USS Nautilus)|label 1=Operation Sunshine}}
[[Dwight D. Eisenhower|President Eisenhower]] ordered the U.S. Navy to attempt a submarine transit of the North Pole as a technological showpiece following the Soviet Union's successful launch of [[Sputnik]].<ref name= IceDiariesFactSheet>{{cite web |url=http://ct.arrl.org/IceDiariesFactSheet.pdf |title=Fact Sheet – USS Nautilus and Voyage to North Pole, August 1958 |last=Anderson |first=William R |access-date=6 September 2012 |archive-date=30 March 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120330182429/http://ct.arrl.org/IceDiariesFactSheet.pdf }}</ref> On 25 April 1958, ''Nautilus'' was underway again for the West Coast under Commander [[William Anderson (naval officer)|William R. Anderson]]. She stopped at [[San Diego]], [[San Francisco]], and [[Seattle]], then began her history-making polar transit under "[[Operation Sunshine (USS Nautilus)|Operation Sunshine]]", leaving Seattle on 9 June. On 19 June, she entered the [[Chukchi Sea]] but was turned back by deep [[drift ice]] in those shallow waters. On 28 June, she arrived at [[Pearl Harbor]] to await better ice conditions.{{Citation_needed|date=August 2019}}

By 23 July, she set a course northward.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.submarinemuseum.org/nautilus/index.shtml |title=Submarine Force Museum, History of USS NAUTILUS (SSN 571) |access-date=10 June 2016 |archive-date=19 June 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160619060331/http://www.submarinemuseum.org/nautilus/index.shtml }}</ref> She submerged in the Barrow Sea Valley on 1 August, and she became the first watercraft to reach the geographic [[North Pole]] on 3 August at 2315 [[Eastern Time Zone|EDT]].<ref name="nautilus.org" /> The ability to navigate at extreme latitudes without surfacing was enabled by the technology of the North American Aviation N6A-1 [[Inertial Navigation System]], a naval modification of the N6A used in the [[SM-64 Navaho|Navaho]] cruise missile; it had been installed on ''Nautilus'' and {{USS|Skate|SSN-578|2}} after initial sea trials on {{USS|Compass Island|AG-153|6}} in 1957.<ref name="Autonetics INS">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1T0NbffwteoC&pg=PA71 |title=Steel Boats, Iron Men: History of the US Submarine Force |publisher=Turner |page=71 |isbn=978-1-56311-081-8 |year=1994 |access-date=6 Sept

Rickover]], known as the "Father of the Nuclear Navy."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.history.navy.mil/bios/rickover.htm |publisher=[[Naval History & Heritage Command]] |title=Biography of Admiral Hyman G. Rickover|access-date=6 September 2012|archive-date=10 February 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120210172002/http://www.history.navy.mil/bios/rickover.htm}}</ref> On 12 December 1951, the Department of the Navy announced that the submarine would be called ''Nautilus'', the fourth U.S. Navy vessel to bear the name. Truman]] on 14 June 1952.<ref>{{Cite AV media |year=1952 |title=Video: Atom Sub. President Officiates At Laying Of Keel, 1952/06/16 (1952) |url=https://archive.org/details/1952-06-16_Atom_Sub |publisher=Universal Newsreels}}</ref> She was christened on 21 January 1954 and launched into the [[Thames River (Connecticut)|Thames River]], sponsored by [[Mamie Eisenhower]]. Nautilus remained dockside after her commissioning for further construction and testing.  At 11:00 a.m. January 17, 1955, the crew dropped the mooring lines and Wilkinson, on the bridge with Rickover, gave the command to back.  When the boat was scarcely clear of the pier, the engineering officer in the maneuvering room reported to Wilkinson on the bridge that there was a loud noise in the starboard reduction gear and that he had switched to electrical propulsion. Under normal circumstances, Wilkinson would have returned at once to the dock, but in full view of the press boats and other small craft attracted to the scene, Rickover was determined not to terminate the trial unless it was necessary.  While the boat proceeded down the river on the port propeller alone, Panoff and the engineering officer inspected the noisy gear.  It took but a few minutes to replace a loose locking pin on a retaining nut, and Wilkinson shifted back to steam propulsion.  As the Nautilus slipped down the Thames past the breakwater into [[Long Island Sound]], a [[Signalman|signalman]] on the submarine blinked to the escort tug [[USS Skylark (ASR-20)|Skylark]]: "Underway on nuclear power."<ref>{{cite web |last=Hewlett/Duncan |first=Richard/Francis |date=June 25, 1973 |title=Nuclear Navy 1946-1962. Richard G. Hewlett and Francis Duncan page 218 |url=https://www.energy.gov/lm/articles/hewlett-and-duncan-nuclear-navy-1946-1962 |access-date=July 22, 2025 |website=energy.gov}}</ref> On 10 May, she headed south for her [[shakedown cruise]]. She traveled {{cvt|1100|nmi|km smi|lk=on|sp=us}} from [[Naval Submarine Base New London|New London]] to [[San Juan, Puerto Rico]] and covered {{cvt|1200|nmi|km smi|sp=us}} in less than 90 hours,<!--(sources differ: 84 hours or 89.8 hours) (I am fact-checking this with USN historian at Groton's Submarine Force Library and Museum --[[User:Pedant]])--><!--Since this is a speed of advance of only 13.33 knots, it's entirely believable --[[User:RobDuch]]--> submerged the entire way. This was the longest submerged cruise by a submarine at the time and at the highest sustained speed ever recorded.{{Citation_needed|date=August 2019}}
[[File:SS-571-Nautilus-trials.gif|thumb|USS ''Nautilus'' during its initial sea trials, 20 January 1955]]

From 1955 to 1957, ''Nautilus'' continued to be used to investigate the effects of increased submerged speeds and endurance. These improvements rendered the progress made in [[anti-submarine warfare]] during [[World War II]] virtually obsolete. [[Radar]] and [[maritime patrol aircraft|anti-submarine aircraft]] had proved crucial in defeating submarines during the war, but they proved ineffective against a vessel able to move quickly out of an area, change depth quickly, and stay submerged for very long periods.<ref>Friedman, Submarines, pp 109</ref>

On 4 February 1957, ''Nautilus'' logged her 60,000th nautical mile ({{cvt|60000|nmi|disp=output only}}), matching the endurance of the fictional [[Nautilus (Verne)|''Nautilus'']] described in [[Jules Verne]]'s novel ''Twenty Thousand Leagues Under The Sea''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.history.navy.mil/research/histories/ship-histories/danfs/n/nautilus-ssn-571-iv.html |title=Nautilus IV (SSN-571) |publisher=[[Naval History & Heritage Command]] |work=[[Dictionary of American Naval Fighting Ships]] |quote=On 4 February 1957, ''Nautilus'' logged her 60,000th nautical mile to bring to reality the achievements of her fictitious namesake in Jules Verne's ''20,000 Leagues Under the Sea.'' |access-date=6 September 2012}}</ref> In May, she departed for the Pacific Coast to participate in coastal exercises and the fleet exercise operation "Home Run," which acquainted units of the [[United States Pacific Fleet|Pacific Fleet]] with the capabilities of nuclear submarines.{{Citation_needed|date=August 2019}}

[[File:GWBridgeUSSNautilus.agr.jpg|thumb|''Nautilus'' passes under the [[George Washington Bridge]] during a visit to [[New York Harbor]] in 1956]]

She then headed for the Eastern Atlantic to participate in [[NATO]] [[Operation Strikeback|exercises]] and to conduct a tour of various British and French ports where she was inspected by defense personnel of those countries. She arrived back at New London on 28 October, underwent upkeep, and then conducted coastal operations until the spring.{{Citation_needed|date=August 2019}}

===Operation Sunshine – under the North Pole===
{{see also|Operation Sunshine (USS Nautilus)|label 1=Operation Sunshine}}
[[Dwight D. Eisenhower|President Eisenhower]] ordered the U.S. Navy to attempt a submarine transit of the North Pole as a technological showpiece following the Soviet Union's successful launch of [[Sputnik]].<ref name= IceDiariesFactSheet>{{cite web |url=http://ct.arrl.org/IceDiariesFactSheet.pdf |title=Fact Sheet – USS Nautilus and Voyage to North Pole, August 1958 |last=Anderson |first=William R |access-date=6 September 2012 |archive-date=30 March 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120330182429/http://ct.arrl.org/IceDiariesFactSheet.pdf }}</ref> On 25 April 1958, ''Nautilus'' was underway again for the West Coast under Commander [[William Anderson (naval officer)|William R. Anderson]]. She stopped at [[San Diego]], [[San Francisco]], and [[Seattle]], then began her history-making polar transit under "[[Operation Sunshine (USS Nautilus)|Operation Sunshine]]", leaving Seattle on 9 June. On 19 June, she entered the [[Chukchi Sea]] but was turned back by deep [[drift ice]] in those shallow waters. On 28 June, she arrived at [[Pearl Harbor]] to await better ice conditions.{{Citation_needed|date=August 2019}}

[[File:SS-571-Nautilus-trials.gif|thumb|USS ''Nautilus'' during its initial sea trials, 20 January 1955]]

These improvements rendered the progress made in [[anti-submarine warfare]] during [[World War II]] virtually obsolete. She arrived back at New London on 28 October, underwent upkeep, and then conducted coastal operations until the spring.{{Citation_needed|date=August 2019}}

[[Dwight D. Eisenhower|President Eisenhower]] ordered the U.S. Navy to attempt a submarine transit of the North Pole as a technological showpiece following the Soviet Union's successful launch of [[Sputnik]].<ref name= IceDiariesFactSheet>{{cite web |url=http://ct.arrl.org/IceDiariesFactSheet.pdf |title=Fact Sheet – USS Nautilus and Voyage to North Pole, August 1958 |last=Anderson |first=William R |access-date=6 September 2012 |archive-date=30 March 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120330182429/http://ct.arrl.org/IceDiariesFactSheet.pdf }}</ref> On 25 April 1958, ''Nautilus'' was underway again for the West Coast under Commander [[William Anderson (naval officer)|William R. Anderson]]. She stopped at [[San Diego]], [[San Francisco]], and [[Seattle]], then began her history-making polar transit under "[[Operation Sunshine (USS Nautilus)|Operation Sunshine]]", leaving Seattle on 9 June. '''USS ''Nautilus'' (SSN-571)''' was the world's first [[nuclear-powered ship|nuclear-powered boat]], [[nuclear-powered submarine]], and the first submarine to complete a submerged transit of the [[North Pole]] on 3 August 1958.  Her initial commanding officer was [[Eugene Parks Wilkinson|Eugene "Dennis" Wilkinson]], a widely respected naval officer who set the stage for many of the protocols of today's Nuclear Navy in the US and who had a storied career during military service and afterwards.<ref>Winters, Ann (28 March 2017). "Underway on Nuclear Power" -- The Man Behind the Words: Eugene P. "Dennis" Wilkinson, Vice Admiral USN. The American Nuclear Society.</ref>

''Nautilus'' shares the name of the [[Nautilus (fictional submarine)|fictional submarine]] in [[Jules Verne]]'s classic 1870 science fiction novel ''[[Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas]]''<ref name="20,000 Leagues Under the Seas">{{cite wikisource |last=Verne |first=Jules |translator=Frederick Paul Walter |title=20,000 Leagues Under the Seas |wslink=20,000 Leagues Under the Seas (Walter) |orig-date=1870 |noicon=yes}}</ref> and the {{USS|Nautilus|SS-168}} that served with distinction in [[World War II]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Nautilus III (SS-168) |url=https://www.history.navy.mil/content/history/nhhc/research/histories/ship-histories/danfs/n/nautilus-ss-168-iii.html |access-date=2021-01-17 |website=NHHC |language=en-US }}</ref>

The ''Nautilus'' was authorized in 1951. Construction began in 1952, and it was launched in January 1954, sponsored by [[Mamie Eisenhower]], wife of President [[Dwight D. Eisenhower]]. It was commissioned the following September into the [[United States Navy]] and was delivered to the Navy in 1955.

Her [[nuclear propulsion]] allowed her to remain submerged far longer than [[Diesel–electric powertrain|diesel-electric]] submarines, and she broke many records in her first years of operation and traveled to locations previously beyond the limits of submarines. In operation, she revealed a number of limitations in her design and construction, and this information was used to improve subsequent submarines.

''Nautilus'' was decommissioned in 1980 and designated a [[National Historic Landmark]] in 1982. She has been preserved as a [[museum ship]] at the [[Submarine Force Library and Museum]] in [[Groton, Connecticut]], where she receives around 250,000 visitors per year.

[[File:Hyman Rickover inspecting USS Nautilus.jpg|thumb|Admiral [[Hyman G. Rickover]] aboard the ''Nautilus'']]
[[File:nautiluscore.jpg|thumb|upright|left|Launching ''Nautilus'']]

The conceptual design of the first nuclear submarine began in March 1950 as project [[Ship Characteristics Board|SCB 64]].<ref>Friedman, Submarines, pp 182</ref><ref>Hewlett & Duncan, Nuclear Navy, pp. 162</ref> In July 1951, Congress authorized the construction of a nuclear-powered submarine for the [[United States Navy|U.S. Navy]], which was planned and personally supervised by Captain [[Hyman G. Rickover]], known as the "Father of the Nuclear Navy."<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.history.navy.mil/bios/rickover.htm |publisher=[[Naval History & Heritage Command]] |title=Biography of Admiral Hyman G. Rickover|access-date=6 September 2012|archive-date=10 February 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120210172002/http://www.history.navy.mil/bios/rickover.htm}}</ref> On 12 December 1951, the Department of the Navy announced that the submarine would be called ''Nautilus'', the fourth U.S. Navy vessel to bear the name.  The boat carried the [[Hull classification symbol|hull number]] SSN-571.<ref name = DANFS>{{cite web |url=https://www.history.navy.mil/research/histories/ship-histories/danfs/n/nautilus-ssn-571-iv.html |title=Nautilus IV (SSN-571) |work=[[Dictionary of American Naval Fighting Ships]] |year=1970 |publisher=[[Naval History & Heritage Command]]}}</ref>

Designers drew inspiration from the advanced hydrodynamic hull design of the [[Type XXI submarine|German Type XXI U-boat]] developed during World War II. The Type XXI U-boat featured a streamlined shape, which enabled greater underwater speed and efficiency compared to earlier submarine designs that were primarily optimized for surface travel. Its revolutionary approach to underwater performance influenced post-war submarine development worldwide, including the U.S. Navy's decision to focus on fully submerged operations.

[[File:nautilus core.jpg|thumb|upright|left|''Nautilus''{{'}}s reactor core prototype at the S1W facility in Idaho]]

''Nautilus''{{'}}s keel was laid at [[General Dynamics]]' Electric Boat Division in [[Groton, Connecticut]] by [[Harry S. Truman]] on 14 June 1952.<ref>{{Cite AV media |year=1952 |title=Video: Atom Sub. President Officiates At Laying Of Keel, 1952/06/16 (1952) |url=https://archive.org/details/1952-06-16_Atom_Sub |publisher=Universal Newsreels}}</ref> She was christened on 21 January 1954 and launched into the [[Thames River (Connecticut)|Thames River]], sponsored by [[Mamie Eisenhower]]. ''Nautilus'' was [[ship commissioning|commissioned]] on 30 September 1954 under the command of Commander [[Eugene P. Wilkinson]].<ref name = DANFS/>

''Nautilus'' was powered by the Submarine Thermal Reactor (STR), later designated the [[S2W reactor]], a [[pressurized water reactor]] produced for the US Navy by [[Westinghouse Electric Corporation]]. [[Bettis Atomic Power Laboratory]] developed the basic reactor plant design used in ''Nautilus'' after being given the assignment on 31 December 1947 to design a nuclear power plant for a submarine.<ref>{{cite press release |url=http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/hn/news960121.shtml |title=Lab's early submarine reactor program paved the way for modern nuclear power plants |work=Argonne's Nuclear Science and Technology Legacy |date=21 January 1996 |publisher=Argonne National Laboratory |access-date=6 September 2012}}</ref> Nuclear power had a crucial advantage in submarine propulsion because it is a zero-emission process that consumes no air. This design is the basis for nearly all of the US nuclear-powered submarines and surface combat ships, and was adapted by other countries for naval nuclear propulsion. The first actual prototype for ''Nautilus'' was constructed and tested by the [[Argonne National Laboratory]] in 1953 at [[S1W reactor|S1W]] at the [[Naval Reactors Facility]], part of the [[Idaho National Laboratory|National Reactor Testing Station]] in Idaho.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/hn/news960121.shtml |title=Argonne National Laboratory News Release, 21 January 1996, retrieved 31 December 2014 |access-date=3 May 2012 |archive-date=27 April 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170427064440/http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/hn/news960121.shtml |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/reactors/lwr3.shtml |title=Reactors designed by Argonne National Laboratory, retrieved 31 December 2014 |access-date=1 January 2015 |archive-date=22 June 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120622185310/http://www.ne.anl.gov/About/reactors/lwr3.shtml |url-status=live }}</ref>

=="Underway on nuclear power"==
Nautilus remained dockside after her commissioning for further construction and testing.  At 11:00 a.m. January 17, 1955, the crew dropped the mooring lines and Wilkinson, on the bridge with Rickover, gave the command to back.  When the boat was scarcely clear of the pier, the engineering officer in the maneuvering room reported to Wilkinson on the bridge that there was a loud noise in the starboard reduction gear and that he had switched to electrical propulsion. Under normal circumstances, Wilkinson would have returned at once to the dock, but in full view of the press boats and other small craft attracted to the scene, Rickover was determined not to terminate the trial unless it was necessary.  While the boat proceeded down the river on the port propeller alone, Panoff and the engineering officer inspected the noisy gear.  It took but a few minutes to replace a loose locking pin on a retaining nut, and Wilkinson shifted back to steam propulsion. Richard G. Hewlett and Francis Duncan page 218 |url=https://www.energy.gov/lm/articles/hewlett-and-duncan-nuclear-navy-1946-1962 |access-date=July 22, 2025 |website=energy.gov}}</ref> On 10 May, she headed south for her [[shakedown cruise]]. This was the longest submerged cruise by a submarine at the time and at the highest sustained speed ever recorded.{{Citation_needed|date=August 2019}}
